title: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
description: Learn how to reduce initial bundle size with React.lazy, Suspense, and dynamic imports.

blocks.text: The Cost of a Monolithic Bundle

By default, bundlers like Vite or webpack bundle your entire application into a single JavaScript file. As your app grows, this bundle becomes larger, increasing the time users wait before they can interact with your page. Code splitting allows you to split the bundle into smaller chunks that load on demand.

Dynamic import() tells the bundler to load a module asynchronously. When you use dynamic import() with React.lazy, React automatically creates a separate chunk for that component and loads it only when it is needed.

blocks.title: Basic React.lazy Usage
blocks.content: Split a heavy dashboard module into its own chunk.

blocks.title: Suspense Is Required
blocks.text: Every lazy component must be wrapped in a Suspense boundary. Suspense displays the fallback UI while the lazy chunk is loading. You can nest multiple Suspense boundaries to provide more granular loading experiences.
Suspense boundaries create loading zones in your UI. When a lazy component is loading, React shows the nearest fallback. This means users can still see parts of the page that have already loaded.

blocks.caption: Suspense boundary behavior
blocks.definition:
graph TD
    A[User Navigates] --> B[App Component]
    B --> C{Suspense Boundary?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Show Fallback UI]
    C -->|No| E[Render Immediately]
    D --> F[Chunk Downloads]
    F --> G[Component Resolves]
    G --> H[Replace Fallback with Content]

blocks.text: Network failures or corrupted chunks can cause lazy components to fail. Wrap lazy imports with an error boundary so users see a helpful message instead of a broken page.

blocks.title: Lazy Load with Error Handling
blocks.content: Combine lazy loading with an error boundary for resilient code splitting.

blocks.text: React.lazy only supports default exports. If you need to lazy-load a named export, create an intermediate module that re-exports it as default.

blocks.title: Lazy Loading a Named Export
blocks.content: Wrap the named export in a module that exports it as default.

items.text: Avoid lazy loading components above the fold

blocks.text: Use tools like Vite's build visualization or webpack-bundle-analyzer to inspect your chunks. Look for unexpectedly large chunks and verify that lazy components are actually generating separate files.
Premature optimization is the root of all evil, but premature pessimization is just as bad.

items.question: Can I lazy load a component that is rendered immediately?
items.answer: Technically yes, but it will hurt performance. The user must wait for the chunk to download before seeing the UI. Only lazy load components that are not immediately needed.

items.question: Does React.lazy work with server-side rendering?
items.answer: React.lazy and Suspense for data fetching are supported in React 18+ with SSR. For component lazy loading on the server, libraries like @loadable/component offer more mature SSR support.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use React.lazy with dynamic import() to split components into separate chunks
Always wrap lazy components in a Suspense boundary
Add error boundaries to handle failed chunk loads
Analyze bundles to confirm your splits are effective
Split by route first, then by feature or component
